question: Which of the following types of trailers is specifically listed by the manual as at risk of getting stuck on a raised railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: A low slung unit such as a lowboy, car carrier, or moving van
choice_b: A flatbed trailer hauling steel coils
choice_c: A refrigerated trailer with high ground clearance
choice_d: A tanker trailer carrying liquid cargo
explanation: The manual lists low slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer) as trailers that can get stuck on raised railroad crossings because of low underneath clearance.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: If your combination vehicle becomes stuck on railroad tracks, what does the manual say to do first?
choice_a: Try to rock the vehicle free before doing anything else
choice_b: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number
choice_c: Stay in the cab with your flashers on and wait
choice_d: Unhook the trailer and drive the tractor off the tracks immediately
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, check signposts or signal housing for emergency notification information, and call 911, giving the crossing location using identifiable landmarks including the DOT number if posted.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: A trailer jackknife caused by locked wheels is more likely to happen when the trailer is:
choice_a: Fully loaded
choice_b: Empty or lightly loaded
choice_c: Equipped with a sliding fifth wheel
choice_d: Carrying liquid cargo
explanation: The manual states that when a trailer's wheels lock up it will tend to swing around, and this trailer jackknife is more likely to happen when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel pull to one side
choice_b: Hearing the trailer brakes squeal
choice_c: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_d: Feeling the trailer bounce
explanation: The manual advises checking your mirrors any time you apply the brakes hard, because seeing the trailer in your mirrors is the earliest and best way to recognize that it has started to skid.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-1

question: What is the correct action to stop a trailer skid once it begins?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake firmly to straighten the rig
choice_b: Release the brakes to let the trailer wheels regain traction
choice_c: Accelerate to pull the trailer straight
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel sharply into the skid
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to stop using the brake and release it to get traction back; once the trailer wheels grip the road again, the trailer will start to follow the tractor and straighten out.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: Why should you never use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out a jackknifing trailer?
choice_a: It is illegal to use in most states
choice_b: The brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place
choice_c: It will drain the air tanks too quickly
choice_d: It only works when the tractor protection valve is closed
explanation: The manual explains this is the wrong thing to do because the brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place, so applying them again will not fix it.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: What term does the manual use for the rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, tighter path than the front wheels when turning a corner?
choice_a: Off-tracking, or "cheating"
choice_b: Crack-the-whip
choice_c: Rearward amplification
choice_d: Drift correction
explanation: The manual defines off-tracking, also called "cheating," as the phenomenon where the rear wheels follow a different path than the front wheels when a vehicle goes around a corner.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: If you cannot complete a turn without entering another traffic lane, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn
choice_b: Turn wide as you complete the turn
choice_c: Stop and back up to reposition
choice_d: Briefly cross into the oncoming lane
explanation: The manual says turning wide as you complete the turn is better than swinging wide to the left before starting it, because swinging wide beforehand invites other drivers to pass you on the right.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-2

question: When backing a trailer, which direction should you initially turn the top of the steering wheel to make the trailer go where you want?
choice_a: The same direction you want the trailer to go
choice_b: The opposite direction of where you want the trailer to go
choice_c: It doesn't matter, only speed matters
choice_d: Always turn it to the right regardless of direction
explanation: The manual explains that when backing a trailer you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from what you would use backing a car, straight truck, or bus, then reverse the wheel once the trailer starts to turn.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: If you must back a trailer on a curved path, to which side should you back?
choice_a: The passenger's side, so a helper can guide you
choice_b: The driver's side, so you can see
choice_c: Either side, since mirrors show both equally well
choice_d: You should never back on a curved path under any circumstance
explanation: The manual recommends positioning your vehicle to back in a straight line whenever possible, and if you must back on a curved path, to back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: What is the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) intended to be used for?
choice_a: Normal service braking while driving
choice_b: Testing the trailer brakes only
choice_c: Parking the combination vehicle
choice_d: Releasing the tractor protection valve
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, and should not be used while driving because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: Why should the trailer hand valve never be used for parking a trailer that lacks spring brakes?
choice_a: It could cause an immediate jackknife
choice_b: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes
choice_c: It voids the warranty on the fifth wheel
choice_d: It unnecessarily engages the ABS system
explanation: The manual warns that on trailers without spring brakes, using the hand valve for parking is dangerous because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes; parking brakes and, if needed, wheel chocks should be used instead.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-3

question: The tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure drops into approximately what range?
choice_a: 0 to 10 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi
choice_c: 60 to 80 psi
choice_d: 90 to 100 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve closes automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi, stopping air from leaving the tractor and setting the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: On newer combination vehicles, what does the trailer air supply control knob look like?
choice_a: A round green button
choice_b: A red eight-sided knob
choice_c: A square yellow lever
choice_d: A blue toggle switch
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as a red eight-sided knob used to control the tractor protection valve.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: What happens when you pull out the trailer air supply control knob?
choice_a: It supplies air to the trailer and releases the emergency brakes
choice_b: It shuts the air off and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: It only activates the ABS system
choice_d: It disconnects the electrical cord automatically
explanation: The manual states you push the knob in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: What is another name given to the trailer service air-line?
choice_a: The control line or signal line
choice_b: The supply line
choice_c: The dummy line
choice_d: The trolley line
explanation: The manual states the service air-line is also called the control line or signal line, and carries air whose pressure is controlled by the foot brake or the trailer hand valve.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-4

question: What are the two purposes of the emergency air-line (supply line) on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It powers the ABS computer and lights the malfunction lamp
choice_b: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: It carries electrical current and operates the turn signals
choice_d: It only supplies air to the parking brakes
explanation: The manual states the emergency line, also called the supply line, has two purposes: it supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and it controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: To help avoid connecting the wrong air-lines, what color is commonly used for the emergency (supply) line, as opposed to blue for the service line?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Yellow
choice_d: Black
explanation: The manual notes emergency lines are often coded with the color red (red hose, red couplers, or other parts) to keep them from getting mixed up with the blue service line.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-5

question: Why does the manual say you should drain each trailer air tank every day?
choice_a: To prevent water and oil buildup from causing the brakes to work incorrectly
choice_b: To reset the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: To recalibrate the tractor protection valve
choice_d: To reduce fuel consumption
explanation: The manual warns that letting water and oil build up in the air tanks may cause the brakes not to work correctly, so each tank should be drained every day even if it has automatic drains.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: When you are pulling a set of trailers, which shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) must be in the closed position?
choice_a: All shut-off valves on every trailer
choice_b: Only the ones at the back of the last trailer
choice_c: Only the ones on the lead trailer
choice_d: None; all shut-off valves must remain open
explanation: The manual states you must check that all shut-off valves are in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: According to the manual, which trailers and converter dollies are NOT required to have spring brakes?
choice_a: Those built on or after March 1, 1998
choice_b: Those built before 1975
choice_c: All trailers manufactured after 2010
choice_d: Only tanker trailers
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes; those without spring brakes rely instead on emergency brakes powered by air stored in the trailer air tank.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: Why is it important to use wheel chocks when parking a trailer that has no spring brakes?
choice_a: The emergency brakes hold only as long as air pressure remains in the trailer air tank, and that air will eventually leak away
choice_b: Chocks are required by federal law regardless of brake type
choice_c: Chocks improve fuel economy while parked
choice_d: Chocks prevent the ABS malfunction lamp from lighting
explanation: The manual explains that trailers without spring brakes rely on emergency brakes held by air pressure in the tank; since that air eventually leaks away leaving no brakes, wheel chocks are essential for safety when parking such trailers.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: January 1, 1995
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: July 1, 2000
choice_d: January 1, 2010
explanation: The manual states that all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS, though many built earlier have been voluntarily equipped with it.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: Trailers required to have ABS must display a malfunction lamp of what color, on which side of the trailer?
choice_a: Red, on the right side
choice_b: Yellow, on the left side, front or rear corner
choice_c: Blue, on the rear bumper
choice_d: Green, near the fifth wheel
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner, and dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998, are also required to have a lamp on the left side.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-6

question: What does the manual say ABS does NOT allow you to do?
choice_a: Drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully
choice_b: Stop the vehicle at all in an emergency
choice_c: Use the trailer hand valve while driving
choice_d: Release the parking brake remotely
explanation: The manual is explicit that ABS won't allow you to drive faster, follow more closely, or drive less carefully; it is only an addition to normal brakes that helps you keep control during hard braking.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: When positioning the tractor to couple with a semitrailer, what does the manual warn against?
choice_a: Backing directly under the trailer in a straight line
choice_b: Backing under the trailer at an angle, which could push it sideways and break the landing gear
choice_c: Checking position using the outside mirrors
choice_d: Putting the tractor in front of the trailer before backing
explanation: The manual instructs putting the tractor directly in front of the trailer, warning never to back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: After backing under the trailer and locking the trailer brakes, how do you check that the coupling is secure?
choice_a: Raise the landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward with the trailer brakes still locked
choice_b: Immediately disconnect the air-lines and check for leaks
choice_c: Accelerate hard in a low gear to test the kingpin
choice_d: Remove the wheel chocks and drive around the yard
explanation: The manual's coupling procedure has you raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground, then pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-7

question: During the final coupling inspection, what should you look for between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: A small visible space, which is normal
choice_b: No visible space; a space means something is wrong with the coupling
choice_c: Grease pooling, which indicates a good connection
choice_d: A gap wide enough to insert two fingers
explanation: The manual says to make sure there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; if there is space, something is wrong, such as the kingpin resting on top of closed fifth wheel jaws, which could let the trailer come loose easily.
source_note: AR CDL Manual (AAMVA 2022 Modernized Testing System, Version: March 2025), Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, p. 6-8
